items.title: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
items.desc: METR reports that leading AI models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra are improving rapidly at research tasks but getting harder to measure. Current data can't rule out a dangerous acceleration in AI development, the organization warns, though it also says common tests may overestimate what the models can actually do. The article AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR , current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems," the organization warns. On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027. The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments. items.title: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
items.desc: The Lean and Mathlib community has officially confirmed Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis as correct. Dozens of independent verifiers checked the 17 million lines of computer code. The solution arrived years earlier than expected: Terence Tao had predicted it wouldn't happen until around 2050 and didn't expect AI to solve it alone. The article Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," the community said in a statement . Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean , a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website . The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper. Ad The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes , forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so." Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
items.desc: Nvidia researchers argue that language models often don't need their full context windows—which are slow, expensive, and prone to errors—and propose an alternative. In tests, periodic summaries and targeted keyword search usually matched full-context results at a fraction of the cost. The team even proposes a new class of models that works with short notes instead of long context. The article Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Language models can now process entire novels at once. An Nvidia research team says that's often overkill and expensive. In many tests, periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well. A language model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply. Over the past few years, that window has grown rapidly. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens. Today, GPT 5.6 Sol handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy's "War and Peace." Already a subscriber? items.title: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
items.desc: A Buddhist monastery in Vermont called Maple wants to establish itself as Silicon Valley's spiritual authority while creating its own AI god. According to a New Yorker report, leader Soryu Forall's group records every breath its members take to train an AI in his image. Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns. The article Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley." Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it. Soryu Forall leads the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or Maple, which he founded in 2011. Forall, who was born Teal Scott, spent years living in Japanese monasteries. According to Kriss's New Yorker report , about two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. While LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs, Maple targets the rank and file: burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers, and data center construction managers. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year. Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism" as a destructive religion. He argues that this worldview strips the physical world down to lifeless data, making the world easier to destroy. In his view, AI is the end product of that logic, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote. Life at the monastery follows a rigid routine. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower, and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours, and then eat a meager stew. On a board outside the meditation hall, Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress. Behind the ascetic facade, former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores." Inside the monastery, AI systems are known as "cybregores." One former member says, "The cybregores are actual entities that are growing by siphoning off the consciousness of humans." Forall says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering. Former members say Maple has two real goals: to establish itself as the tech industry's spiritual authority and to use the industry's resources to build its own "dharmically aligned" AI. Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal, and even the sound of their breathing. According to these accounts, the recordings are meant to train a spiritual AI teacher that would guide other AI systems to enlightenment. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says it would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god." Maple's leadership denies almost all of these claims. Forall, however, acknowledges that there is a secret doctrine: "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy." items.title: Symphony Review: A Team of AI Agents for the Business Behind Your Website
items.desc: You can keep your WordPress site in good shape yet still lose leads to unanswered emails, missed follow-ups, and an out-of-date calendar. My Symphony review looks at a team of AI agents, led by one orchestrator, that can organize your work and wait for approval. The post " Symphony Review: A Team of AI Agents for the Business Behind Your Website " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: To be a small business owner is to spin multiple plates at once: lead generation, client outreach, general marketing and sales, design, and much more. Often, some of those plates will fall and smash, which might mean you lose a good prospect, don’t hit a deadline, or myriad other negatives. By the end of this Symphony review, you might choose to take a breath and let its Maestro orchestrator organize your work tasks, so you can sweep up the broken crockery! Each of Symphony’s four pricing tiers comes with the core functionality of Maestro and the ability to use multiple AI agents around the clock. The difference between each plan is the number of AI credits you receive per month, the ‘activity level’ of your agents, the number of actions you have available, and your usage allocation. Here are the three premium plans: The cost I give here is based on annual billing. A month-by-month subscription costs slightly more. There aren’t any exact figures on the activity level of your agents and usage allocation either, just that higher tiers give you more. Free is more of an extended taster of what Symphony can give you. There’s an allocation of 500 credits per month and 100 daily credits. I think the Free plan is a generous offering given what’s included in the premium tiers. You also get two agent actions and briefings. If your credits run out before the month’s end, agents pause the work and wait for your credit allocation. It means you won’t need to adapt to an unfinished workflow or lose any work. If you run a small business, there are a few concerns you likely have regularly: This is what Symphony aims to improve. In a nutshell, you chat with Maestro (the orchestrator) and after it learns about your business, it dishes out the work to a set of AI agents. Each agent has one area of responsibility, but you can add custom agents if you need to work on a specific task. Wix claims the agent knowledge comes from 300 million businesses across a variety of regions and industries. Symphony is platform-agnostic , which means you don’t need to run a Wix site to use it (although you do need a Wix account). Instead, it connects to your calendars, email account, CRM, MCP server, and other tools. My first impression is that Symphony is going to be most helpful for single-person businesses or small teams. Freelancers or content creators fit the bill, but agencies that run several projects at once can also benefit. The Pro plan is likely the best fit for all of these business types. A freelancer with a small workload could opt for Basic, but you wouldn’t want to restrict your growth based on your Symphony plan. There are four core aspects to Symphony that cover the majority of your needs: Everything works through human-language prompts , and each project gets its own contained workspace. For instance, you can tell Maestro the details of your business and it assembles a team of AI agents based on the suitability for the task. It covers outreach and marketing, scheduling, research, design, and even finance. The information is also used to build a knowledge base, which involves a constant learning cycle. items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra solved a math theorem no other AI could crack, then invented its own proof strategy
items.desc: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra independently produced a machine-verifiable Lean proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem, the first of its kind according to Vals AI. The model chose its own approach because key foundations were missing from Mathlib. On Autoform-Hard, Astra now leads the leaderboard with 49 of 56 tasks solved. The article GPT-6.2 Astra solved a math theorem no other AI could crack, then invented its own proof strategy appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produced a formalized, machine-verifiable proof of a 2006 theorem with zero human help during the run. According to Vals AI , it's the first known proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem written in Lean . The theorem states that when a mathematical system multiplies its basic building blocks, growth is either quite slow or very fast. There's no middle ground. Because key foundations of the original proof were missing from the math library Mathlib, Astra took a different route than the published mathematical proofs , Vals says. It used "capacity," a metric from existing research that checks the minimum number of elements added per computation step. This happened on Autoform-Hard , a subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench curated by Vals. It contains 56 tasks (five corrected) that ten models in Meta's study failed to solve within budget. When Astra tried to quit after 47 minutes and eight dollars, the system rejected the attempt since unsolved submissions aren't accepted until $20 has been spent. After nine minutes of silence with no code input while it searched for a new strategy, Astra delivered the 1,800-line proof at the 94-minute mark for $21.58. It now leads the leaderboard with 49 solved tasks, ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 at 48 each. Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.full: Follow the show in your app Apple Podcasts (WP Minute+ Podcast) Spotify (WP Minute+ Podcast) YouTube (WP Minute+ Podcast) Overcast (WP Minute+ Podcast) RSS (WP Minute+ Podcast) AI is changing how we build websites, develop plugins, and even think about the future of WordPress. But is the WordPress community ready for what’s coming? In this special episode of The WP Minute, Matt Medeiros sits down with Dan Maby, co-founder of Show.fm, to discuss the rapid changes happening across the WordPress ecosystem and what they mean for developers, agencies, and the wider community. Dan shares his perspective on the challenges facing WordPress events, the growing influence of AI, and the risks of building software without thinking about long-term maintenance, security, and sustainability. They also dig into the hidden costs of AI, the potential for vendor lock-in, and why being able to build something doesn’t always mean you should. Then, the conversation shifts to podcasting. Dan explains how he and Nathan Wrigley evolved Podcaster Plus into Show.fm, an end-to-end podcast operations platform designed to help creators manage everything from guest booking to publication. They explore guest discovery, automations, analytics, AI-powered research, and the importance of owning your content through RSS. Is WordPress at a crossroads? Is AI creating more work than it’s solving? And can podcasting become a more sustainable business? Let’s get into it. New articles and episodes, plus the week’s WordPress news. A five-minute read. items.title: Meta's Alexandr Wang warns the AI industry isn't ready for what's coming after Riemann breakthrough
items.desc: Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang sees the recent AI-assisted proof sketch of the Riemann Hypothesis as a clear sign that superintelligence is right around the corner. The article Meta's Alexandr Wang warns the AI industry isn't ready for what's coming after Riemann breakthrough appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang sees the recent AI-assisted proof sketch of the Riemann Hypothesis as a clear sign that superintelligence is right around the corner. The Riemann Hypothesis is widely considered the most intellectually demanding unsolved problem in mathematics. The brightest minds have failed to crack it for 150 years. The fact that an AI model played a major role in the breakthrough shows that raw intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, Wang argues. According to Wang, current models only lack domain-specific knowledge and practical infrastructure to outperform humans in nearly every field. That includes AI research itself. Since AI research is intellectually less demanding than the Riemann Hypothesis, Wang believes models could soon automate their own development and improve themselves. They could also dramatically speed up biological research, weapons research, and economic research at a pace humans can barely follow. Wang also warns that the AI industry isn't thinking hard enough about what comes next. In his view, many in the field treat superintelligence as inevitable and focus only on safety. But the stakes are much broader than that, he argues. The industry needs to actively ensure that AI gives people more agency rather than taking control of society. That would require a sharp departure from the current course, Wang says. Despite having its own superintelligence team , Meta isn't a major player at the frontier right now.
